Notes:
1. Consolidated financial statements are prepared in accordance with the International Financial Reporting Standards (“IFRS”).
2. Figures presented are rounded down to the nearest million yen.
3. Upon the adoption of IFRS, the Ajinomoto Group has introduced “Business profit” as a new profit level that will better enable
    investors, the Board of Directors, and the Executive Committee to grasp the core business results and future outlook of each
    business while also facilitating continual evaluation of the Group’s business portfolio by the Board of Directors and the
    Executive Committee. “Business profit” is defined as sales and share of profit of associates and joint ventures minus cost of
    sales, selling expenses, research and development expenses, and general and administrative expenses. Business profit does not
    include other operating income or other operating expenses.
4. In the 147th Fiscal Year, the Company finalized the provisional accounting treatment for a business combination, and the
    finalized figures have been reflected in the 146th Fiscal Year.
5. With a 2-for-1 stock split of the Company’s ordinary shares effective April 1, 2025, equity per share (attributable to owners of the
    parent company), basic earnings per share and diluted earnings per share were calculated based on the assumption that the stock
    split was conducted at the beginning of the 144th Fiscal Year.

                                                                  -2-
2. History
   Month/Year                                                     Overview
May 1907         Established Suzuki Pharmaceutical GSK.
July 1908        Dr. Kikunae Ikeda obtained a patent for the production method of seasoning (monosodium glutamate). In
                 September of the same year, Saburosuke Suzuki II undertook the commercialization.
May 1909         Launched umami seasoning AJI-NO-MOTO®.
April 1912       Suzuki Pharmaceutical GSK. succeeded to the AJI-NO-MOTO® business, operated as a personal business of
                 Suzuki, and changed the company name to Suzuki Shoten GSK. at the same time.
September 1914   Completed the Kawasaki factory and started operation.
June 1917        Established S. Suzuki & Co. Ltd. and transferred all business of Suzuki Shoten GSK. to the said company,
                 and changed the business purpose of Suzuki Shoten GSK. to the acquisition and sale of securities and real
                 estates.
December 1925    Established S. Suzuki Co., Ltd. and transferred all business of Suzuki Shoten GSK. and S. Suzuki & Co.,
                 Ltd. to the said company, and dissolved these two companies. (present Ajinomoto Co., Inc.)
October 1932     Changed its company name to Ajinomoto Honpo S. Suzuki & Co., Ltd.
March 1935       Established Takara Oil Refining Co., Ltd. and started fat and oil business.
December 1940    Changed its company name to Suzuki Shokuryo Kogyo Co.
May 1943         Changed its company name to Dai-Nippon Chemical Co.
December 1943    Established the Saga factory in Saga prefecture. (present Kyushu Plant)
May 1944         Merged Takara Oil Refining Co., Ltd.
February 1946    Changed its company name to Ajinomoto Co., Inc.
May 1949         Listed on the stock market.
January 1956     Launched essential amino acids (for infusion) and started amino acid business.
July 1956        Established Ajinomoto Co. of New York, Inc. (present Ajinomoto Health & Nutrition North America, Inc.)
December 1956    Set up a central research laboratory in Kanagawa prefecture.
May 1958         Established Union Chemicals Inc. (present AJINOMOTO PHILIPPINES CORPORATION)
April 1960       Established Ajinomoto Co., (Thailand) Ltd.
March 1961       Set up a Yokkaichi factory in Mie prefecture. (present Tokai Plant)
July 1961        Established Ajinomoto (Malaya) Co., Ltd. (present Ajinomoto (Malaysia) Berhad)
March 1963       Entered into partnership with U.S.’s Corn Products International. (present Conopco, Inc.) (founded a joint-
                 venture company, Knorr Foods Co., Ltd.)
October 1967     Set up Specialty Chemicals Department and fully started specialty chemicals business.
February 1968    Established Ajinomoto del Perú S.A.
July 1969        Established PT Ajinomoto Indonesia.
November 1970    Launched HON-DASHI®.
December 1970    Established Ajinomoto Restaurant Foods Co., Inc. (present Ajinomoto Frozen Foods Co., Inc.) and started
                 frozen food business.
August 1973      Entered into partnership with U.S.’s General Foods Corporation. (founded a joint-venture company, present
                 Ajinomoto AGF, Inc.)
December 1974    Established Ajinomoto Interamericana Indústria e Comércio Ltda. (present Ajinomoto do Brasil Indústria e
                 Comércio de Alimentos Ltda.)
September 1981   Launched ELENTAL® and started pharmaceutical business.
May 1982         Launched export of aspartame and started sweeteners business.
June 1987        Made Knorr Foods Co., Ltd. a subsidiary.
September 1989   Acquired all shares of a Belgian chemical company S.A. OmniChem N.V. (present S.A. Ajinomoto
                 OmniChem N.V.)
December 1996    Established Ajinomoto (China) Co., Ltd.
October 2000     Spun off the frozen food business into a separate company and integrated it into Ajinomoto Frozen Foods
                 Co., Inc.
April 2001       Spun off the fat and oil business into a separate company and integrated it into Ajinomoto Oil Mills Co., Inc.
                 (present J-Oil Mills, Inc.)
February 2003    Ajinomoto Frozen Foods Co., Inc. acquired all shares of Frec Co., Ltd. from Nippon Sanso Ltd., and merged
                 with Frec Co., Ltd. in April 2003.
July 2003        Acquired all shares of ORSAN SA (present Ajinomoto Foods Europe S.A.S.), an umami seasoning
                 production and sales company held by Amylum France S.A.S.
February 2007    Acquired part of shares of Yamaki Co., Ltd. and entered into a capital and business alliance.
November 2011    Transferred operation of feed-use amino acid business to Ajinomoto Animal Nutrition Group, Inc.
                 (established in September 2011)


                                                          -3-
   Month/Year                                                   Overview
November 2014   Ajinomoto North America, Inc. acquired all equity interest of Windsor Quality Holdings, LP, a frozen food
                manufacturing and sales company in the U.S.
April 2015      Ajinomoto Frozen Foods U.S.A., Inc. merged Windsor Quality Holdings, LP and changed its company name
                to Ajinomoto Windsor, Inc. (present Ajinomoto Foods North America, Inc.)
April 2015      Made Ajinomoto General Foods, Inc. (present Ajinomoto AGF, Inc.) a subsidiary.
April 2016      AJINOMOTO PHARMACEUTICALS CO., LTD., engaged in the pharmaceutical business, succeeded a
                part of the business in the area of digestive diseases of Eisai Co., Ltd. through an absorption-type company
                split, became an affiliate accounted for by the equity method of the Company and changed the company
                name to EA Pharma Co., Ltd.
November 2016   Acquired 33.33% shares of Promasidor Holdings Limited, a major processed foods manufacturer that
                conducts business in countries in Africa and made it an affiliate accounted for by the equity method of the
                Company.
April 2019      Concentrated and reorganized the production system of part of the Kawasaki factory and Tokai Plant and
                Ajinomoto Packaging Co., Inc. to Knorr Foods Co., Ltd. and changed its company name to Ajinomoto Food
                Manufacturing Co., Ltd.
July 2021       Merged Ajinomoto Animal Nutrition Group, Inc.
December 2023   Ajinomoto North America, Inc. acquired all equity interest of Forge Biologics Holdings, LLC (present Forge
                Biologics, Inc.), a US-based gene therapy CDMO.




                                                        -4-
3. Description of business
 The Ajinomoto Group consists of Ajinomoto Co., Inc., 105 consolidated subsidiaries, and 15 affiliates accounted
 for by the equity method, and is engaged in areas of Sauce & Seasonings, Quick Nourishment, Solution &
 Ingredients, Frozen Foods, Amino Acids for Pharmaceuticals and Foods, Bio-Pharma Services (CDMO
 services), Functional Materials (electronic materials and others), as well as other business activities.
 The position of the said Group’s business is as follows. (Companies marked with asterisks (*) are affiliates
 accounted for by the equity method.)

II.          Overview of Business
1. Management policy, business environment, issues to address
      The management policy, business environment, and issues to address of the Ajinomoto Group are as follows.
      Note that matters related to future developments that are mentioned in this section are judgments of the
      Ajinomoto Group that were made as of the end of the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026 (on a consolidated
      basis).
      <Continuously strengthening our ability to execute Our Philosophy*1>
      In FY2025, the Ajinomoto Group refined its strategies, from the company-wide level through to business and
      functions, grounded on our Purpose—contributing to the well-being of all human beings, our society and our
      planet with “AminoScience”—and guided by ASV (Ajinomoto Group Creating Shared Value)*2 and the
      Ajinomoto Group Way (AGW)*3. It was a year in which we focused squarely on “Thinking well based on our
      Purpose, envisioning with a healthy sense of urgency, and executing with a proper approach,” while genuinely
      building the people and organizations needed to bring our Purpose to life. Through initiatives such as the group-
      wide implementation of My Purpose Workshops*4, we are connecting each individual’s purpose to specific
      goals and challenges, thereby enhancing engagement*5. As we reach the midpoint of our Medium-term ASV
      Management 2030 Roadmap, we will continue to evolve our four intangible assets—human resources,
      technology, customers, and organization—which serve as the source of value creation, along with our corporate
      culture. By further enhancing our ability to envision and execute, we will steadily build on daily challenges
      aimed at achieving sustainable growth.
      *1 “Our Philosophy” is a systematization of the most important principles in the Ajinomoto Group’s corporate activities: Purpose,
         ASV, AGW.
      *2 ASV represents our unchanging commitment: With our stakeholders and businesses, we help solve society’s issues, leading to
         the creation of economic value.
      *3 The values, fundamental principles, and mindset that guide how each employee works: create new value, pioneer spirit, social
         contribution, and value people.
      *4 A program where employees explore and articulate their own aspirations, their “My Purpose,” and find overlaps with the
         Ajinomoto Group’s purpose, “Our Purpose.”
      *5 Deepening employees’ attachment to the Company and their work, as well as their willingness to contribute.




      In addition, in pursuit of our two key outcomes by 2030—“Reducing our environment impact by 50%” and
      “Helping extend the healthy life expectancy of 1 billion people”—we will not only steadily reduce negative
      impacts through our business activities, but also leverage our strength in “AminoScience” to develop and
      deliver technologies, expertise, products, and services that create a positive impact for society.




                                                                 - 13 -
<Important issues (Materiality) for the Ajinomoto Group>
The Ajinomoto Group has identified important issues (Materiality) that are essential to its ability to continue
co-creating social and economic value over the long term.
Through extensive discussions with a broad range of stakeholders, and based on the value creation framework
(approach), the Ajinomoto Group has identified Six Material Themes to be addressed in relation to the value
that the Group is expected to provide to various stakeholders and to society.




<Three years into the Medium-term ASV Management 2030 Roadmap>
Three years have passed since the Ajinomoto Group announced its “Medium-term ASV Management 2030
Roadmap” in February 2023, which outlines our vision for 2030 and the path to achieving it through backcasting*6.
In implementing the Roadmap, we abolished the more conventional three-year medium-term management plan
that we had in place and instead are working to steadily drive organic growth and create new businesses through
business model transformation, centered on the “challenging targets set by management” (ASV indicators*7)
guided by our long-term vision. This is being pursued by combining both forecast*8 perspectives based on existing
businesses, and backcast approaches aligned with our future aspirations.
*6 Backcasting is a method of envisioning how to achieve a goal by “working backward” from a desirable future
   to the present as a means of determining what one should do now.




                                                     - 14 -
*7 Indices that encourage further growth and aspiration, consisting of economic value indicators that
   demonstrate the degree to which the Ajinomoto Group’s business has performed financially, as well as social
   value indicators that are intended to measure the value that the Group strives to create on a societal level.
*8 A way of thinking that predicts the future as an extension of the present.

<Advancing ASV management centered on seven company-wide strategies and strengthening the
execution framework>
Under Mr. Shigeo Nakamura’s new leadership structure introduced in February 2025, we have been working to
further develop our ASV management centered on company-wide strategies reflecting the progress made under
the Medium-term ASV Management 2030 Roadmap. Specifically, we have designed and implemented seven
company-wide strategies aligned with the “Seven Important Management Matters” presented by the Board of
Directors: Medium- to Long-Term Growth Strategy; Portfolio Strategy; Financial and Capital Strategy; Speed
Up x Scale Up of Organizational Execution Abilities; Sustainability Strategy; Stakeholder Engagement; and
Strengthening of Corporate Governance and Compliance. Through this approach, we are enhancing resource
allocation and decision-making across businesses, functions, and regions. We believe that human resources,
organization, and corporate culture form the foundation supporting the execution of these company-wide
strategies. Accordingly, under the new executive structure introduced in April this year, a Chief Human
Resources Officer (CHRO) position has been established to integrate responsibility for both company-wide
strategies and human resources and organizations. In addition, by strengthening the expertise and execution
capabilities of management functions, we have been able to establish a framework aimed at further advancing
ASV management. Going forward, while appropriately responding to changes in the business environment, in
FY2026 we will particularly focus on optimizing our portfolio, strengthening intangible assets, including
human resources and organizational capabilities, and evolving organizational management. Through these
efforts, we aim to steadily and sustainably enhance our corporate value as a company that contributes to the
well-being of all human beings, our society and our planet.




                                                  - 16 -
To enhance our corporate value, in “steadily generate cash flow,” the numerator of the Ajinomoto Group’s
standard calculation of corporate value, we will refine both our growth potential and earning power, such as
organic growth, EBITDA margin improvement, the implementation of ROIC-focused management, the
improvement of cost efficiency, such as for raw material and manufacturing costs, appropriate inventory
management, and the enhancement of supply chain management (SCM). In the denominator, “capital cost
reduction,” we will utilize sustainable finance by promoting sustainability, strengthening risk management,
reducing borrowing costs, and utilizing appropriate financial leverage. In “growth rate increase,” we will
enhance our ability to envision and execute short-, medium-, and long-term business strategies. We will also
realize further Speed Up x Scale Up. With our standard calculation of corporate value in mind, we will continue
to innovate, strive, and challenge ourselves within each organization, and as a whole Group, we will continue to
pursue the creation of value that transcends organizational boundaries.




                                                    - 17 -
2. Disclosure of sustainability-related financial information
   <Our approach to sustainability>
   The Purpose of the Ajinomoto Group is to contribute to the well-being of all human beings, our society and our
   planet with “AminoScience.” We position sustainability at the core of ASV management. We aim to drive
   sustainability initiatives in an integrated manner with our business strategy, creating both social and economic
   value to achieve sustainable business growth and enhance corporate value. We advance specific initiatives that
   address both risks and opportunities under the Medium-term ASV Management 2030 Roadmap. These efforts
   align with the Six Material Themes identified as important issues (Materiality) for the Ajinomoto Group.
   The Ajinomoto Group’s business depends on sound agrifood systems that produce and consume food resources,
   and on the rich global environment that supports this system. This system both faces environmental changes
   and contributes significantly to the loss of natural capital. Adapting to these changes and restoring nature are
   urgent priorities for society and for the sustainable growth of our business as the global environment nears its
   limits. To this end, we advance efforts in climate change, biodiversity, the circular economy, and respect for
   human rights, aiming to reduce the negative impacts of our business activities and strengthen the resilience of
   our business foundation. We also implement various initiatives to help achieve better nutritional balance,
   greater emotional well-being through food, and progress in both prevention and treatment. These efforts are
   expected to enhance people’s well-being while creating growth opportunities through value creation leveraging
   “AminoScience.”
   The Ajinomoto Group not only works to steadily reduce negative impacts through business activities but also
   aims to create stronger positive impacts across—and also beyond—the value chain by leveraging our strengths
   in “AminoScience” and working with diverse stakeholders. Furthermore, through these initiatives, we aim to
   strengthen the resilience of our business foundation while creating growth opportunities, thereby contributing to
   the realization of a prosperous and healthy society and healthy and richer lives, while also striving to
   sustainably increase our corporate value.
   Forward-looking statements in the text below are based on the Group’s assessments as of March 31, 2026.

* Based on the recommendations of the Second Sustainability Advisory Council, the Board of Directors
  will continue dialogue with external experts and convene the next Sustainability Advisory Council at
  an appropriate time.


The Board of Directors determines important issues (Materiality) for the Ajinomoto Group that serve as
guidelines for ASV management, and supervises the formulation of sustainability strategies and the
execution of initiatives. For example, it deliberates on the medium- to long-term sustainability strategy as
one of its important management matters, and exchanges opinions with external experts based on the
recommendations of the Sustainability Advisory Council.
The Sustainability Advisory Council was established as a subordinate body of the Board of Directors
with the aim of making recommendations to enhance the corporate value of the Ajinomoto Group from
the viewpoint of sustainability. In the second phase of the Sustainability Advisory Council, which
commenced in April 2023, the council assessed the efforts of the Board of Directors in the areas of
Materiality implementation, communication on implementation and information disclosure, and
partnership building with stakeholders. The council submitted their final report to the Board of Directors
in March 2025. The final report highlighted expectations for strengthening partnership building with
stakeholders in order to deliver greater value beyond the scope of a single company. In response, for
FY2025, the council set two themes: sustainability-related rulemaking and sustainable finance, including
consideration of collaboration with international organizations and financial institutions. It also held two
rounds of discussions between Directors and external experts, with the outcomes of these discussions
shared with the Executive side.
The Executive Committee has established the Sustainability Committee and the Risk Management
Committee as subordinate bodies and selects and extracts risks and opportunities based on important
issues (Materiality) for the Ajinomoto Group, formulating measures, and managing progress. In FY2025,
the Executive Committee received four activity reports from the Sustainability Committee and two from
the Risk Management Committee.

                                               - 20 -
    The Sustainability Committee works with the Risk Management Committee to select and identify risks
    and opportunities based on Materiality as well as assess their impact on the Ajinomoto Group, making
    proposals to the Executive Committee. The Sustainability Committee then explores and formulates
    countermeasures for sustainability risks and opportunities and manages their progress. In addition, the
    Sustainability Committee formulates the entire Ajinomoto Group’s sustainability strategy, promotes
    action based on this strategy, makes proposals and provides support for business plans from a
    sustainability viewpoint, and compiles internal information on ESG.
    The Risk Management Committee works with the Sustainability Committee to select and identify risks
    and opportunities based on Materiality as well as assess their impact on the Ajinomoto Group, making
    proposals to the Executive Committee. The Risk Management Committee also develops and manages the
    progress of risk management measures to establish a strong corporate structure that ensures prompt and
    accurate responses to risks and crises, particularly with regard to risks that management should address
    (e.g., geopolitical risks, information security risks).


(2) Strategy
    With the global environment nearing its limits, addressing environmental changes can no longer be
    postponed. It is our duty to ensure that the next generation can inherit a flourishing global environment
    and healthy society, which are essential to the sustainable growth of the Ajinomoto Group’s business.
    Stabilizing the climate is a particularly urgent issue, and it is strongly required that we become nature
    positive—that is, stop the loss of nature and put nature on the road to recovery. We must also
    comprehensively address other mutually connected issues, such as circular economy, nutritionally
    balanced diets, and human rights.
    The Ajinomoto Group procures around 70% of its materials from the agricultural, livestock, and fishery
    industries, and therefore is highly dependent on the agrifood systems, which itself is supported by the
    bounty of nature, or in other words, ecosystem services. The agrifood system accounts for more than 20%
    of all GHG emissions and is the second highest emitter behind the energy industry. Although on the one
    hand it has a significant impact on the global environment, it is also vulnerable to direct impact from
    environmental changes such as climate change and the loss of natural capital. Moreover, around one-third
    of all food produced globally is wasted, and around one-third of the global population, or 2.8 billion
    people, do not have access to healthy food. These structural issues represent both significant risks and
    opportunities for value creation through transformation for the Ajinomoto Group.
    As above, there is significant room for change in the agrifood systems. At the Ajinomoto Group, we have
    been working on building a biocycle to transform fermentation byproducts into fertilizer and feed,
    circulating nutrients to support the production of agricultural and livestock products, and improving both
    the global environment and QOL for farmers. Based on these activities, more recently we have been
    working on businesses that reduce environmental impact, restore nature, and improve food productivity
    in the agricultural and livestock industries. Moreover, throughout our 110-year history, we have
    supported nutritionally balanced food through products and solutions, in line with global food cultures
    and without compromising on taste. In addition to the nutritional benefits of food, it has also become
    clear through global studies that cooking and eating with others is linked to subjective well-being.
    The Ajinomoto Group is engaged in a wide range of businesses based on its proprietary strength,
    “AminoScience,” including the Food Products business, which includes seasonings, processed food
    products, and frozen foods, as well as healthcare and electronic materials. Moving forward, we will
    continue to make use of our tangible and intangible assets and work with scientists, policymakers,
    business leaders, and other global and local stakeholders to steadily reduce negative impacts. At the same
    time, we will aim to create more positive impacts for society throughout—and also beyond—the value
    chain, aiming to strengthen the resilience of our business foundation while creating growth opportunities.
    We consider human assets to be the source of all our intangible assets and fundamental to the above
    activities. We have therefore positioned employee engagement as a key factor to improving corporate
    value. Through human resource investments, we will enhance our execution ability of purpose-driven
    management by ASV initiatives by ensuring that our diverse human resources with purpose can work
    more closely with consumers and customers to co-create innovation, thereby contributing to the well-
    being of all human beings, our society and our planet.

(3) Risk management
     To achieve the Medium-term ASV Management 2030 Roadmap, we must identify risks accurately and
     respond to these risks promptly and appropriately. The Sustainability Committee and the Risk
     Management Committee work closely together to ensure no risk is left unaddressed between the two. The
     committees select and identify risks and opportunities based on important issues (Materiality) for the
     Ajinomoto Group and propose these risks and opportunities to the Executive Committee. The
     Sustainability Committee formulates response measures and manages progress on matters related to
     sustainability. The Risk Management Committee handles risks that require management attention (e.g.,
     geopolitical risks and information security risks).
     We implement risk management processes at each domestic and overseas work site to identify risks and
     formulate countermeasures, taking individual business strategies and local political, economic, and social
     conditions into account. The Risk Management Committee improves these processes and compiles the
     risks identified by each work site and addresses those that management should take the initiative to
     address. In addition, each business and corporation has formulated a business continuity plan (BCP) in
     preparation for emergencies and the Risk Management Committee has established a system for constant
     verification of each BCP’s effectiveness and manages the risk response. Full-time Audit Committee
     members attend the Sustainability Committee and the Risk Management Committee to monitor risk
     management process.


(4) Metrics and targets
     The Ajinomoto Group is currently addressing Six Material Themes (see page 18), and has set targets and
     KPIs that take into account the risks and opportunities that may arise through its business operations, in
     line with these themes for the reduction of negative impacts, such as environmental impact, and for the
     creation of positive impacts across society as a whole using its proprietary strength, “AminoScience.”
     The Executive Committee is responsible for checking the progress and performance of the Ajinomoto
     Group’s main initiatives. Please see “Focus areas, initiatives and targets/KPIs related to important issues
     (Materiality) for the Ajinomoto Group” (page 43) for initiatives, targets, and KPIs related to all the Six
     Material Themes.

      The Company’s governance for climate change issues is as described in <Our approach to

(2) Strategy
      The Ajinomoto Group has a wide range of product areas in the Food Products business, from seasonings
      and foods to frozen foods, and is also expanding its business into fields such as healthcare. Climate
      change affects the Group’s business in many ways, including delays to business due to large-scale natural
      disasters, impact on procuring raw materials such as agricultural produce and fuels, and changes in
      product consumption.

      (i)     Scenario analysis assumptions
              Based on the scenarios that the average global temperature will rise from post-industrial revolution
              levels by 1.5°C or 4°C by 2100*1, in FY2025, we again conducted a scenario analysis on the impact
              of climate change between 2030 and 2050 for global umami seasonings and mainstay domestic and
              overseas products.
              Among the effects of climate change impacting production over the medium and long term,
              drought, floods, rising sea levels, and changing yields of raw materials were analyzed as physical
              risks, while the introduction of carbon pricing and tightening of other laws and regulations, rising
              energy prices, and changes in consumer preferences were analyzed as transition risks.
              The tables in (ii) and (iii) show risks and opportunities, respectively, in scenario analysis when the
              average temperature difference between the 1.5°C and 4°C scenarios as of 2030 is considered to be
              about 0.2°C with no significant difference in physical risk, and when the average temperature
              difference as of 2050 is expected to be about 1°C with differences in physical risks.

        (iv) Reflecting scenario analysis results in strategy
            a.    Reflection in our business strategy
                  Based on the impact of the scenario analysis on our business, we plan to invest in fossil fuel
                  phase-out and the use of renewable energies, as well as eco-friendly manufacturing methods to
                  further reduce our greenhouse gas emissions in the future. We will also work on formulating
                  new business strategies to achieve ASV, where sustainability initiatives lead to greater added
                  value for our products.
                  We will review risks and opportunities in scenario analyses for FY2026 and beyond, based on
                  updated data from various sources.
            b.    Reflecting on financing strategy
                  Sustainable finance forms the basis for acquiring the necessary funds for our various initiatives.
                  Beginning with the issuance of sustainable bonds in October 2021, we have continued to
                  procure funds through sustainable finance. Our efforts here include securing a commitment line
                  agreement through positive impact financing in January 2022 (renewal with increased amount
                  in January 2024), a commitment line agreement through Sustainability Linked Loans in
                  December 2022 (renewal in December 2025), and the issuance of Sustainability Linked Bonds
                  in June 2023*5. Most recently, we issued two new sustainability-linked loans in March and
                  April of 2024.
                  Through this financing, we will further accelerate our efforts to realize one of our two outcomes
                  by 2030, namely, to reduce our environment impact by 50%, as well as to realize a sustainable
                  society.

(ii) FY2025 results
    Total Scope 1 and 2 greenhouse gas emissions for FY2025 decreased by nearly 123,000 t-CO2e
    from the previous fiscal year. This reduction was driven by the procurement of renewable energy
    certificates by P.T. AJINOMOTO INDONESIA.
    Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions (covering all categories) decreased by approximately 5% year on
    year. This result was due to the use of more primary data on raw materials and improved calculation
    accuracy. Emissions declined by 21% compared to the base year of FY2018, reflecting a decrease in
    the Ajinomoto Group’s total production volume (excluding retrospective adjustments for emissions
    from businesses that left the Ajinomoto Group after the base year).




    Our reductions in Scope 1 and 2 emissions and Scope 3 emissions (excluding Category 11)
    retroactively adjusted to include emissions from companies excluded from the Ajinomoto Group
    after FY2019 in accordance with SBTi standard, in relation to the SBTi-approved Scope 1 and 2
    emissions target (-50.4% vs. FY2018) and Scope 3 emissions target (-30% vs. FY2018; excluding
    Category 11) for FY2030, were 49% and 15%, respectively. For Scope 1 and 2, we are on track to
    achieve approximately 90% of our target in our current plan. However, we will consider further
    reduction activities to achieve even greater emissions reductions. For Scope 3, we will continue our
    efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions through primary data collection and reduction initiatives
    enabled by deeper engagement with Scope 3 raw material suppliers, as well as through joint
    procurement of low-greenhouse-gas raw materials.

         [Disclosure of our measurement methods, etc. for greenhouse gas emissions]
              The Ajinomoto Group measures greenhouse gas emissions in accordance with company rules based
              on the Greenhouse Gas Protocol Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard (2004) (“GHG
              Protocol (2004)”). Activity data for Scope 1, 2, and 3 are mainly based on figures for production
              sites. We note that the quantification of greenhouse gas emissions is subject to uncertainties
              regarding the measurement of activity data, the determination of emission factors, and scientific
              uncertainties regarding the determination of the global warming potential (GWP).
             a.    Scope 1 greenhouse gas emissions
                   Scope 1 greenhouse gas emissions are calculated by multiplying the activity data for the fiscal
                   year ended March 31, 2026 by the emission factors specified in the Ministry of the
                   Environment’s latest List of Calculation Methods and Emission Factors in the Calculation,
                   Reporting, and Publication System available as of March 31, 2026.
             b.    Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions (market-based)
                   For the Ajinomoto Group domestic sites, we measured Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions using
                   a market-based estimation method in which we multiplied the amount of electricity used for
                   each electricity contract during the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026 by the emission factor for
                   each electricity contract, as provided in the Ministry of the Environment’s latest Emission
                   Factors by Electricity Utility available as of March 31, 2026.
                   For the Ajinomoto Group overseas sites, we measured Scope 2 greenhouse gas emissions using
                   a market-based estimation method in which we multiplied the amount of electricity used for
                   each electricity contract during the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026 by the latest country-
                   specific emission factor from the International Energy Agency (IEA) available as of March 31,
                   2026.
                   Of note, our calculations reflect electricity derived from renewable energy, non-fossil fuel
                   certificates, and I-RECs, etc., that are deemed to meet the quality requirements based on the
                   GHG Protocol Scope 2 Guidance and other standards.
             c.    Scope 3 greenhouse gas emissions
                   The Ajinomoto Group, in accordance with company rules, measures Scope 3 greenhouse gas
                   emissions for the main Scope 3 categories using the following activity data and emission factors
                   based on our estimation method.
                   Category 1 (Purchased goods and services): Measured based on an estimation method in which
                   the production volume at each manufacturing site is multiplied by the carbon footprint of
                   product (CFP) unit value of the relevant product or applicable product for raw materials and
                   packaging at the raw material (including packaging) stage as the emission factor.
                   Category 4 (Upstream transportation and distribution): Measured based on an estimation
                   method in which the production volume at each manufacturing site is multiplied by the CFP
                   unit value of the relevant or applicable product at the transportation stage (upstream (raw
                   materials), downstream (products) where the Company bears the cost) as the emission factor.
                   Category 11 (Use of sold products): Measured based on an estimation method in which the
                   production volume of frozen foods, cup soups, instant noodles, and instant coffee among

                                                       - 29 -
         domestic and international products is multiplied by the CFP unit value at the CFP use stage for
         each product as the emission factor.
         *    For Scope 3 Category 1, primary data is used for some main raw materials.


(iii) Efforts to achieve targets
     Our measures to meet our Scope 1 and 2 targets include conducting energy-saving activities,
     switching to fuels with low greenhouse gas emissions, using renewables such as biomass and solar
     power, and introducing processes to lower energy consumption (e.g., procurement of renewable
     energy certificates at Group companies in Japan).
     For Scope 3 targets, raw materials are causing approximately 60% of total greenhouse gas
     emissions over the whole product life cycle. Therefore, we encourage raw materials suppliers to
     reduce their greenhouse gas and consider introducing new technologies and reducing greenhouse
     gas emissions through agricultural initiatives centered on regenerative agriculture.

<Our approach to biodiversity>
(1) Governance
     The Company’s governance for biodiversity is as described in <Our approach to sustainability>.

(2) Strategy
     The Ajinomoto Group offers a wide range of products in the Food Products business, from seasonings
     and food products to frozen foods. We are also expanding into healthcare and other fields. Our businesses
     heavily depend on the bounty of nature, such as agriculture, livestock, and fishery resources, genetic
     resources, water, soil, and pollinators such as insects. These natural bounties come from healthy
     biodiversity shaped by the diversity of living organisms and their connections. However, biodiversity is
     currently being lost at an unprecedented rate, making biodiversity conservation, prevention of
     deforestation, and conservation of water resources pressing issues worldwide. In April 2025, the
     Ajinomoto Group revised the Ajinomoto Group Biodiversity Guidelines. Since issues related to
     biodiversity conservation, prevention of deforestation, and conservation of water resources are also
     closely related to environmental boundaries and social issues such as climate change, water and soil,
     waste, and human rights, we will work to resolve these issues so as to create mutual benefit.

     (i)    LEAP approach
            The LEAP approach is guidance proposed by the Task Force on Nature-related Financial
            Disclosures (TNFD) that provides a process for the systematic, science-based assessment of nature-
            related risks and opportunities within corporations and financial institutions.
            In FY2023, we used the LEAP approach to assess risks and opportunities based on an analysis of
            dependencies and impacts in eligible businesses of the Ajinomoto Group. In FY2024, we conducted
            a detailed analysis of sugar cane (the Assess step), physical risk of which has significant financial
            impacts. In FY2025, we launched a joint initiative with the Indonesian Sugar Research Institute
            (ISRI/P3GI) to evaluate farming methods that support both improved farmer livelihoods and
            environmentally responsible sugar cane production.
           a.   Selection of target raw materials
                From among the raw materials in our businesses that provide 80% coverage of net sales, we
                selected 12 raw materials that are listed under High Impact Commodity List (HICL) provided
                by SBTs for Nature, and that have a large procurement volume. For this analysis, we selected
                sugar cane, cassava, corn, raw milk, soybeans, rapeseed, rice, cattle, coffee, palm, copper, and
                crude oil. Note that we excluded paper (packaging material), which is considered an HIC
                material.

              c.    Results of detailed sugar cane analysis
                    Sugar cane was one of raw materials with the highest level of risk in the above three-step LEA
                    analysis. We therefore conducted a detailed analysis of sugar cane in Thailand, Indonesia, and
                    Brazil, where there is expected to be a significant loss of nature by 2050. Specifically, for all
                    sugar cane procurement mills, we conducted a database analysis of water risk, deforestation
                    risk, and soil degradation risk at four random farming areas within sugar cane procurement
                    zones, with a focus on each sugar cane mill. Our analysis showed that the relatively high
                    deforestation risk areas where sugar cane mills are located are Banyuwangi, Jember,
                    Pekalongan, and Pemalang in Indonesia, and Sukhothai in Thailand.
                    In FY2025, we launched a joint initiative with the Indonesian Sugar Research Institute
                    (ISRI/P3GI) to evaluate farming methods that support both improved farmer livelihoods and
                    environmentally responsible sugar cane production based on the results of our field survey of
                    water risk, deforestation risk, and soil degradation risk in sugar cane farmlands.

<Our approach to human capital>
(1) Governance
     The Company’s governance for human capital is as described in <Status of corporate governance, etc.>
     In addition, we have established the Human Resources Committee as a subordinate body to the Executive
     Committee, with the aim of promoting matters related to human resource development that support the
     sound growth of the Ajinomoto Group. The Human Resources Committee is chaired by the CEO or an
     Executive Officer designated by the CEO, with members consisting of Executive Officers designated by
     the CEO. The Committee deliberates on matters related to the selection of Executive Officer candidates,
     the development of management human resources and human resource leaders, the certification and
     appointment of Corporate Executives and Group Executive Managers (a total of 120 positions as of
     March 31, 2026), and the formation of a diverse human resource base. A total of 7 discussions were held
     in FY2025.


(2) Human resources strategy
     To realize our Purpose—contributing to the well-being of all human beings, our society and our planet
     with “AminoScience”—the Ajinomoto Group must promote the co-creation of social and economic value
     through ASV (Ajinomoto Group Creating Shared Value) and engage in the AGW (Ajinomoto Group
     Way), our systematized code of conduct that support this.
     The Ajinomoto Group’s growth strategy involves building a solid foundation for growth in the Food
     Products business, achieving dramatic growth in the Bio & Fine Chemicals business, and creating new
     value in the Convergence Areas of both businesses. To achieve this, we must utilize “AminoScience” as
     a source of competitive strength and combine it with our unique Deliciousness Technology cultivated in
     the food area, scientific knowledge in health and medicine, and advanced technologies represented by our
     Electronic Materials and Bio-Pharma Services, and integrate them as a growth driver.
     To ensure the execution of this growth strategy, we need to enhance our business portfolio and
     restructure our global human resources portfolio accordingly, while maintaining a balance between
     autonomous and decentralized operations at global sites and businesses and centralized operations at our
     head office. It is important to interconnect our four intangible assets (human resources, technology,
     customers, and organization), which serve as the source of this growth, and to scale them as execution
     abilities. We are therefore particularly strengthening our initiatives for human assets, which link
     technology assets and customer assets and generate innovation.
     Each of our diverse employees who have empathy for the Ajinomoto Group’s Purpose takes on
     challenges going beyond their comfort zones to enhance their own capabilities of executing strategies.
     Furthermore, by leveraging such individual capabilities, we also promote diversity (DE&I*8) from the
     perspectives of knowledge, experiences, and attributes to create innovation as a team. The cornerstone
     supporting all of this is the well-being of our employees and their families. The Ajinomoto Group is
     rolling out global initiatives for human assets under the concept of the four connecting strategies of
     connecting Purpose, challenge, diversity (DE&I), and well-being. (Human resource investment amount
     (including opportunity investment): ¥15.0 billion in FY2025; total of more than ¥100.0 billion between
     2023 and 2030). We believe that these initiatives will not only enrich our human assets, but will also
     build as organization assets, thereby enriching our intangible assets overall.

         Of the four connecting strategies, we are steadily advancing initiatives related to Purpose and well-being
         on a global scale. On the other hand, we recognize that the challenge and diversity (DE&I) strategies
         present relatively greater challenges and require more focused strengthening.

         Issues related to challenge:
         The strong growth of our Electronic Materials business under the Bio & Fine Chemicals business is
         supported by our High-speed Development System. To expand this High-speed Development System to
         other areas as a driving force for new businesses and products, strengthening the underlying challenging
         spirit in our corporate culture is essential. If we do not sufficiently foster a challenging spirit in our
         company culture, this could delay our expansion into growth areas, potentially impacting the
         achievement of the challenging ASV indicators set forth in our 2030 Roadmap.

         Issues related to diversity:
         To achieve new regional and new product development in the Food Products business and dramatic
         growth in the Bio & Fine Chemicals business, we must organically integrate the diversity of the
         Ajinomoto Group from the perspectives of knowledge, experiences, and attributes. If we do not make
         progress with diversity integration, there is a risk that the acquisition of new knowledge and experiences
         will be delayed.




                                                            - 35 -
Connecting company and human resources with Purpose
As the Ajinomoto Group operates various businesses across the globe, one material theme we must
address is how to enhance the unifying force that brings together Group strengths as our businesses and
regions expand. As a source of this unifying force, we are working to increase empathy for Our
Philosophy with an eye to making ASV as one’s own initiative. As part of this initiative, the Ajinomoto
Group has introduced an ASV management cycle comprising the following steps: Understanding and
Sense-making; Empathy and Resonance; Execution and Realization; and Monitoring and Improvement.
In FY2025, we continued to implement the “My Purpose Workshop,” where employees articulate their
own purpose and find overlap with the Ajinomoto Group’s Purpose. We also developed the “Our
Philosophy Challenge,” a simulation-based workshop where employees learn through hands-on
experience about business creation and solving social issues powered by “AminoScience,” starting from
their own aspirations. Through cross-departmental co-creation and challenges, we aim to enhance our
execution ability of Our Philosophy and develop human resources who can turn their purpose into
concrete action. As a result of these initiatives, in our engagement survey (“ES”), the score for Purpose
(comprised of a total of seven questions including “I support values that are the company’s guiding
principles”) was 89 (a one-point increase year-on-year).




Connecting strategy and human resources with challenge
The strong performance of our Electronic Materials business under the Bio & Fine Chemicals business,
which has significantly driven sales and business profit growth, is supported by our High-speed
Development System. The High-speed Development System is a method that enables us to respond to
rapid changes in the market and customer environment through three Key Success Factors: (1) anticipate
customer needs, (2) rapidly develop multiple solutions, and (3) continuously improve solutions based on
feedback. This approach is applicable not only to the Electronic Materials business but also to other
businesses and functions. As such, we believe it will serve as the driving force for achieving our
challenging ASV indicators for 2030, and even for creating new businesses and products beyond that.
Supporting the achievement of this, the heightened desire for challenge that comes from articulating the
overlap between the Purpose of the Ajinomoto Group and the purpose of each individual employee.
Ajinomoto Co., Inc. is expanding its self-nomination transfers and TRY&A-CROSS (internal side-job
program) as opportunities to take on new challenges. These initiatives are also being implemented at
Group companies, including those overseas. The score for challenge in our ES (comprised of a total of
six questions including “My supervisor encourages me to learn from mistakes”) was 87 (a one-point
increase year-on-year). To further strengthen a challenging spirit in our company culture, we consider all
daily activities that aim for continuous growth and strive to be even slightly better than yesterday,
without putting off what you can do today until tomorrow, as taking on challenges. To support diverse
challenges in line with AGW, we will promote the operation of systems that appropriately connect
challenges and results.




                                              - 36 -
Connecting globally diverse human resources
The Ajinomoto Group, primarily in the Food Products business, has demonstrated strong adaptability to
local markets by addressing the culture and preferences of each region, enabling individual Group
companies to expand their businesses autonomously. This local market adaptability is a strength that
drives the current growth of the Food Products business. Meanwhile, for long-term business expansion, it
is essential that we expand into new regions and countries and introduce new products in the Food
Products business, and create new areas in the Bio & Fine Chemicals business. To achieve this, we
believe it is important to promote DE&I from the perspective of knowledge, experiences, and attributes
to enhance our team’s execution abilities and generate innovation.
We made steady progress with the diversity of the Ajinomoto Group’s leadership (Executive Officers,
Corporate Executives, and Group Executive Managers: 137 positions) in terms of gender, nationality, and
affiliation, etc., which reached 27% in FY2025. We have created succession plans for the relevant
positions using three timeframes, Ready (1–3 years), Next (within 5 years), and Future (within 8 years).
In doing so, we are forming a pool of human resources for next-generation leaders and strengthening
strategic development and appointment.
Furthermore, Ajinomoto Co., Inc. is working to recruit mid-career hires from the perspective of acquiring
expertise in new and growth areas. In FY2025, the recruitment rate of mid-career hires among all new
employees hired in a single year was 40%, and the ratio of employees joining as mid-career hires as a
share of all employees was 20%. In addition, while the ratio of female managers at Ajinomoto Co., Inc.
increased by 2% year-on-year to 16%, it remained low compared to the ratio of female employees (33%),
an indication that the creation of a pipeline of female managers remains an issue. To address this, we are
promoting measures to support the development of women who are non-managers, such as AjiPanna
Academy. In the FY2025 training, 97% of the 43 participants expressed their aspirations of becoming
managers. Furthermore, ES results showed that more than half of female employees are motivated to take
on higher positions, with the score reaching 70% for women in their 20s and 30s (a 4% increase year-on-
year). Moreover, the ratio of female employees in their 30s also increased to 36%, and the ratio of female
employees in their 20s is on an uptrend at 40%. We thus believe that the ratio of female managers will
gradually improve. To further accelerate the integration of knowledge and experiences, it is important
that we allocate the right number of right persons in the right position at the right time, from a global
perspective. The Ajinomoto Group has established guidelines for international transfers and is promoting
transfers not only between Japan and overseas sites but also between overseas sites. To further enhance
their effectiveness, we are working to clarify the best human resource portfolio to align with our business
portfolio, and to establish human resource policies and guidelines that apply globally.


Connecting human resources and well-being
In terms of physical and mental health, we are globally promoting Health and Productivity Management
(H&PM), aiming to ensure that working at the Ajinomoto Group naturally makes employees healthier.
From the perspective of financial well-being, our Group companies are aiming to establish competitive
compensation structures benchmarked against the external compensation market across relevant regions
and businesses. As a result of these efforts, the well-being score in our ES (comprised of seven questions
including “There are efforts for nutrition improvement at the workplace” and “I am receiving fair
compensation”) was 85 (a one-point increase year-on-year).

Key KPI: Monitoring the ASV realization process through the ES
As a key KPI to measure the results of human capital investments based on our four connecting
strategies, the Ajinomoto Group is globally monitoring the ASV realization process in our ES. In
FY2025, the ASV realization process score was 78 (a two-point increase year-on-year), falling short of
our FY2025 target of 80.
The main reason for not meeting the target was that the score for the question related to the company-
wide issue of enhancement of productivity (approval process issues), “I think that in this company, we
have to get a lot of approvals before making decisions in our daily work,” showed a significant nine-point
improvement from the previous year, but still remained low. To understand the root cause, a new
question was introduced in FY2025: “I think that unnecessary approvals are kept to a minimum for
decision-making in daily work.” The score for this new question was 78. This result confirmed that while
there are many approvals, a large number of respondents do not perceive them as unnecessary from the
perspective of governance or business and product quality.


                                              - 37 -
         Based on this, from FY2026, questions related to the enhancement of productivity (approval process
         issues) in the ASV realization process will be replaced with new questions. Meanwhile, since issues
         regarding the excessive amount of prior explanation and ambiguity of approval criteria were raised in the
         open-answer section, we will continue to work on making improvements. Furthermore, in conjunction
         with these question changes, we have raised our FY2030 target score for the ASV realization process
         from 85 to 88.

3. Business and other risks
   (1) Risks and opportunities related to important issues (Materiality) for the Ajinomoto Group
         The Purpose of the Ajinomoto Group is to contribute to the well-being of all human beings, our society
         and our planet with “AminoScience.” We position sustainability at the core of ASV management. Based
         on this approach, the Group identified 16 topics in relation to its Six Material Themes (materiality) and
         organized group-wide risks and opportunities that require cross organizational management as shown in
         the table below.
         The topics, risks and opportunities were identified by considering not only their potential effects and
         likelihood, but also their relevance to the Group’s Purpose and business strategy. In addition, the results
         of impact assessments conducted by the Risk Management Committee were also considered.
         Specifically, the Group referred to and considered the disclosure topics set forth in the SASB Standards,
         including “Processed Foods,” “Biotechnology & Pharmaceuticals,” and “Semiconductors,” and, in order
         to complement macro-environmental changes that cannot be fully captured by these topics alone, also
         referred to external reports on the global economy, geopolitics, regulatory trends, technological
         developments, and industry trends. Furthermore, taking into account the Ajinomoto Group’s business
         characteristics and the uncertainties in its business environment, the Group defined relevant topics and
         conducted research and analyses of events that could represent potential risks or opportunities for the
         Group. These identifications and judgments are based on information available and assumptions
         considered reasonable as of the date of preparation of this Securities Report. The Group will conduct
         periodic reviews as necessary in response to changes in its business environment and operations. Please
         refer to Disclosure of sustainability-related financial information - (1) Governance, on roles of
         Sustainability Committee and Risk Management Committee.

4.   Management analysis of financial position, operating results and cash flows
     Overview of results
     Upon the adoption of IFRS, the Ajinomoto Group has introduced “business profit” as a new profit level that
     will better enable investors, the Board of Directors, and the Executive Committee to grasp the core business
     results and future outlook of each business while also facilitating continual evaluation of the Group’s business
     portfolio by the Board of Directors and the Executive Committee. “Business profit” is defined as sales and
     share of profit of associates and joint ventures minus cost of sales, selling expenses, research and development
     expenses, and general and administrative expenses. Business profit does not include “Other operating income”
     or “Other operating expenses.”
     Forward-looking statements in the text below are based on our assessments as of March 31, 2026.


     (1) Management’s analysis and discussion of operating results
          Financial and capital strategies supporting changes to the business portfolio
          To realize its Vision for 2030, the Ajinomoto Group is promoting stable growth based on the Food
          Products business, dramatic growth in the Bio & Fine Chemicals field, and new value creation in
          Convergence Areas. The core that supports these growth strategies consists of strengthening our cash
          flow generation capabilities and maintaining consistent investment discipline to reliably turn generated
          cash into long-term value.
          To strengthen our cash flow generation capabilities, we must invest in fields expected to see further
          growth, carry out M&As in fields that will undergo dramatic growth, and divestitures in fields without
          prospects for competitive advantage. As EBITDA rises, we can also significantly increase our debt
          capacity and use this additional capacity to fund further growth investment. To maintain consistent
          investment discipline that reliably turns generated cash into long-term value, we must firmly strengthen
          our human resources and governance. There are various strategies for the initiatives used to support this
          growth. Here, we would like to touch on four of these strategies.
          The first is FP&A human resource investment to support our strategies. Acquiring and deploying the
          global expertise of our Financial Planning & Analysis (FP&A) team to support our business growth
          (Strategy 1) is the very embodiment of human resource investment. The FP&A team uses DX and AI to
          evolve rolling forecasts and contribute to the enhancement of corporate value by providing advice about
          future risks and opportunities to management in a timely fashion.
          Next, carrying out M&As backed by financial perspectives (Strategy 2) and consistent disposal of
          businesses is vital for growth to achieve our vision. We will strive to increase shareholder value by
          carrying out M&As and disposing of businesses based on financial perspectives.
          In addition, global tax management is an important part of our financial strategy. Our strategy and
          implementation team, which excels at tax management, will participate in major capital investment and
          M&A projects from their first stages, creating optimal tax payment structures and lowering effective tax
          rates.
          Lastly, responsible governance that supports growth is vital for proper growth. To support global Group
          management, we will thoroughly comply with and refine 30 policies, procedures, and guidelines related
          to finance and capital, curbing limitations on our growth while maximizing the value we create.




                                                        - 46 -
<Vision for 2030 and strategies for realizing it>




(i)   Status of individual metrics for 2030 Roadmap
      Led by the concepts of our corporate value calculation formula, we consider future cash flow
      maximization and capital cost optimization to be fundamental to the enhancement of corporate
      value. To enhance corporate value over the medium to long term, we promote management that is
      focused on balancing profitability, growth, capital efficiency, and financial soundness.




      In FY2025, the Ajinomoto Group set new records for net sales and business profit, surpassing the
      records set last year. Business profit continued to grow by a double-digit percentage, rising for the
      seventh consecutive year. This growth was led by the Healthcare area, which consists primarily of
      Functional Materials and Bio-Pharma Services (CDMO services), and profit also increased for the
      Food Products business, which includes Seasonings and Foods and Frozen Foods. Revenue
      increased steadily for the portfolio as a whole.
      Furthermore, we are maintaining a high level of cash generation backed by revenue growth, with
      operating cash flow surpassing the previous year at ¥239.3 billion, a new record. Our financial base,
      which supports our sustained growth investment and shareholder returns, has been further
      strengthened.
      As for our ASV indicators for 2030, in FY2025, our ROE was 17.7%, ROIC was 11.8%, organic
      sales growth was 3.7%, and EBITDA margin ratio was 17.1%. In all of these, we have made steady

                                               - 47 -
     progress towards our medium- and long-term targets, and our capital efficiency and profitability
     have reached the level at which it appears we may reach our targets ahead of schedule.
     To optimize our cost of capital, our basic policy is to both improve capital efficiency and maintain
     financial soundness, and we have set the net interest-bearing debt/EBITDA ratio as our key
     financial discipline indicator. In FY2025, in addition to steadily increasing EBITDA, we
     compressed our surplus funds, bringing the ratio to 1.6x and maintaining it within the target range
     (<2.0x), as we appropriately controlled leverage.
     Regarding capital allocation, we actively implemented growth investments, including investments
     in intangible assets, focusing on strengthening our cash generating capacity predicated on business
     growth. In FY2026, we plan to invest roughly ¥130.0 billion as capital investment, to accelerate our
     investment in next-generation growth areas, and to further improve our cash generating capacity by
     improving our working capital.
     As for shareholder returns, we will continue to pay stable dividends based on normalized EPS, led
     by our progressive dividend policy. The total return ratio (to profit attributable to owners of the
     parent company), including the purchase of treasury shares, for the three-year period is set at 50%
     or more. Next year, we also plan to continue increasing dividends and give back to shareholders
     with an eye towards improving capital efficiency and maximizing shareholder value.
     Note:    Dividends based on normalized EPS = (Business profit × (1 − Ajinomoto Group standard
              tax rate at 27%)) / Total number of shares outstanding × Return coefficient at 35%


     <Targets defined in 2030 Roadmap and their progress>




(ii) Capital allocation policy
     Our capital allocation policy is based on creating returns that exceed the weighted average cost of
     capital (WACC).
     First, we focus the allocation of capital to investment aimed at achieving sustained organic growth
     and M&As, etc., for realizing dramatic growth. We then allocate remaining cash to shareholder
     returns through the purchase of treasury shares, etc. This is our fundamental capital allocation
     policy.
     To achieve sustained organic growth, we have positioned the reinforcement of our business
     foundation and capital investment aimed at increasing returns as important investments. In FY2026,
     we plan to invest approximately ¥130.0 billion as capital investment. We are also considering
     M&As aimed at creating synergy with existing businesses for Convergence Areas and acquiring

                                              - 48 -
     new opportunities for dramatic growth. As with our acquisition of Forge Biologics, Inc. in FY2023,
     we plan to continue to actively invest in M&A projects that contribute to dramatic growth.
     For fields with diminished prospects for competitive advantage, on the other hand, we will
     strategically reallocate resources, including selling off businesses. We will continuously review our
     allocation of capital based on the assumption that customers, competitors, and business
     environments will change. We will further refine our capital allocation through deliberations in
     newly established company-wide growth strategy meetings that take into consideration the balance
     of growth potential, profitability, and risk.




(iii) Measures to generate cash flow
     Generating cash flow requires not only capital investment but also investment in intangible assets,
     including human capital. We always share our diverse measures that contribute to the generation of
     cash flow with our Group and global human resources. This ultimately contributes to our human
     resource investment and, we believe, produces a positive management cycle. For these purposes, we
     plan to use our FP&A human resources who have experience with global business management, to
     further increase our value. Below are some examples of the measures we have implemented.

     First, we present our initiative to improve EBITDA margins by revising inventory-counting methods.
     In our production plants, shipments are sometimes limited for periods of time due to physical
     inventory counts performed as part of audits. We are switching to cycle-count stocktaking, which
     does not interrupt production, instead of physical stocktaking, to eliminate these shipment restrictions,
     increase sales, and help improve our EBITDA margin.
     Next, let’s look at our FP&A initiatives in the North American Consumer Foods Business. We are
     performing simulations from various perspectives, such as plant-specific, category-specific, channel-
     specific, and marginal profit-specific simulations, and providing our management team with analysis
     results for maximizing our company’s cash flow.
     Last, let’s look at our “stop, reduce, and change” activities. This is a fundamental framework for
     improving operations in Japan. We are striving to reduce excess costs, eliminate waste, and allocate
     the resources freed up to further our growth. With an eye toward stopping, reducing, and changing
     existing work, we are also utilizing AI to make proactive improvements. Through these initiatives,
     we are reducing time spent on operations and shifting resources to work that can generate higher
     corporate value. In fiscal 2025, we engaged in over 600 “stop, reduce, and change” activities.


                                               - 49 -
          <Examples of measures to generate cash flow>




          A message to shareholders and investors
          We will continue to engage in highly profitable, highly efficient growth investment, further improve
          efficiency, and refine and evolve our business risk management while carefully managing capital
          allocation. Our CEO, Shigeo Nakamura, and our management team will strive to improve our
          sustained corporate value and achieve long-term results, with tripling EPS by FY2030 (vs. FY2022)
          in mind.


(2) Production, orders received, and sales
     The Ajinomoto Group produces and sells a broad and diverse range of products. Even for similar types of
     products, their forms and units are not necessarily the same, while some products are used in other
     segments within the Group as raw materials. Moreover, as we do not have many made-to-order products,
     we do not show the scale of production and orders received in terms of amount or quantity for each
     segment.
     As such, results for production, orders received, and sales are shown in relation to segment results in “(4)
     Analysis of operating results.”

           The Ajinomoto Group’s consolidated financial statements are prepared in accordance with the

           Consolidated Financial Statements and Notes, (1) Consolidated Financial Statements.” The estimates

     (4) Analysis of operating results
           During the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026, the Company’s consolidated sales increased 3.5% year on
           year, or ¥53.1 billion, to ¥1,583.7 billion. This was due to increases in sales in the Seasonings and Foods
           segment and the Healthcare and Others segment.
           Business profit increased 13.7% year on year, or ¥21.8 billion, to ¥181.1 billion, primarily due to
           increased revenue from the Healthcare and Others segment and the Seasonings and Foods segment.
           Operating profit increased 75.0% year on year, or ¥85.4 billion, to ¥199.4 billion. This was mainly due to
           recording of gain on sale of non-current assets as a result of the transfer of a portion of the Company’s
           non-current assets (the land and building of the head office) during the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026,
           in addition to higher business profit.
           Profit attributable to owners of the parent company totaled ¥134.6 billion, up 91.6%, or ¥64.4 billion, due
           to the increase in operating profit and other factors.

Overview of each section of the consolidated statements of income
(i)   Sales
      Sales were up 3.5% or ¥53.1 billion to ¥1,583.7 billion. In Japan, sales increased 8.8% or ¥46.1
      billion to ¥571.7 billion. Overseas sales grew by 0.7% or ¥6.9 billion to ¥1,011.9 billion. In Asia,
      the Americas, and Europe, sales were up 5.2% to ¥464.6 billion, down 7.9% to ¥382.4 billion, and
      up 11.4% to ¥164.9 billion, respectively. The overseas share of sales decreased to 63.9% from
      65.7% in the previous fiscal year. Note that sales are attributed to the location of sale, and are
      classified by country or region.

(ii) Cost of sales, selling expenses, research and development expenses, general and administrative
     expenses, and share of profit of associates and joint ventures
      As sales increased, the cost of sales rose by 0.7% or ¥6.7 billion to ¥986.5 billion, equivalent to
      62.3% of sales. The ratio of cost to sales improved by 1.7 percentage points year on year. Selling
      expenses increased 6.3% or ¥13.3 billion to ¥225.3 billion, mainly due to increased advertising
      expenses and foreign exchange effects. Research and development expenses increased 3.8% or ¥1.1
      billion to ¥32.1 billion. General and administrative expenses increased 7.6% or ¥11.7 billion to
      ¥166.6 billion, due notably to increased employee benefit expenses and foreign exchange effects.
      The Group’s share of profit of associates and joint ventures totaled ¥8.1 billion compared to ¥6.3
      billion in the previous fiscal year.

(iii) Business profit
      Business profit grew 13.7% or ¥21.8 billion to ¥181.1 billion. In Japan, business profit increased
      26.5% to ¥93.2 billion. Overseas business profit grew by 6.2% to ¥133.6 billion. In Asia, the
      Americas, and Europe, business profit was up 4.7% to ¥91.9 billion, up 5.8% to ¥26.9 billion, and
      up 16.8% to ¥14.6 billion, respectively. The overseas share of business profit decreased to 73.7%
      from 79.0% in the previous fiscal year. Note that business profit is attributed to the location of sale,
      and is classified by country or region.
      For details on business profit by segment, please see “V. Financial Information, 1. Consolidated

(iv) Other operating income and expenses
      Other operating income increased 884.3% or ¥43.6 billion to ¥48.5 billion, mainly due to a
      recording of gain on sale of non-current assets as a result of the transfer of a portion of the
      Company’s non-current assets (the land and building of the head office). Other operating expenses
      decreased 39.6% or ¥19.9 billion to ¥30.3 billion, mainly due to the recording of impairment loss on
      goodwill and non-current assets related to Althea in the preceding fiscal year.

      Operating profit grew 75.0% or ¥85.4 billion to ¥199.4 billion.

      ¥2.1 billion to ¥12.3 billion.

      billion, equivalent to ¥138.36 per share, up from ¥69.77 in the previous fiscal year.
